body.back: The smallest particle of an element that can exist and still show the chemical properties of that element.
body.front: What is an atom?
body.hint: Atom = smallest unit of an element

body.back: A substance made of one type of atom only; it cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.
body.front: What is an element?

body.back: Charge +1; relative mass 1.
body.front: Relative charge and relative mass of a proton

body.back: Charge 0; relative mass 1.
body.front: Relative charge and relative mass of a neutron

body.back: Charge -1; relative mass 1/1840 (negligible).
body.front: Relative charge and relative mass of an electron

body.back: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are in shells (energy levels) surrounding the nucleus.
body.front: Where are protons, neutrons and electrons found in an atom?

body.back: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
body.front: Define proton (atomic) number.

body.back: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
body.front: Define nucleon (mass) number.

body.back: Number of neutrons = nucleon (mass) number minus proton (atomic) number.
body.front: How do you calculate the number of neutrons?

body.back: It has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so the charges cancel.
body.front: Why is an atom electrically neutral?

body.back: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
body.front: Define isotopes.

body.back: They have the same number of electrons, and so the same electronic configuration.
body.front: Why do isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties?
Give the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11).

body.back: In order of increasing proton (atomic) number.
body.front: How are elements arranged in the Periodic Table?

body.back: It equals the group number (Groups I to VII) and determines the element's chemical properties.
body.front: What does the number of outer-shell electrons tell you about an element?

body.back: Solid, liquid and gas.
body.front: Name the three states of matter.
body.hint: SLG: from most ordered to least ordered.

body.back: Particles are closely packed in a regular arrangement (lattice).
body.front: Describe the arrangement of particles in a solid.

body.back: Particles vibrate about fixed positions.
body.front: Describe the movement of particles in a solid.

body.back: Particles are close together in an irregular arrangement and move past each other (slide over one another).
body.front: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid.

body.back: Particles are far apart, in a random arrangement, and move quickly in random directions.
body.front: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a gas.

body.back: Change of state from solid to liquid; occurs at the melting point when particles gain enough energy to overcome forces holding them in a lattice.
body.front: Define melting.

body.back: Change of state from liquid to gas, occurring at the boiling point throughout the liquid, with bubbles forming.
body.front: Define boiling.

body.back: Evaporation occurs at the surface at any temperature below the boiling point; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at the boiling point only.
body.front: Difference between evaporation and boiling?

body.back: Change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.
body.front: What is sublimation?

body.back: Energy absorbed is used to overcome forces between particles, so temperature stays constant during the change of state.
body.front: What happens to particle energy when a substance is heated during melting?
body.hint: Flat line on a heating curve.

body.back: In gases the particles are far apart with large spaces between them; in liquids and solids particles are already close together.
body.front: Why can gases be compressed easily but liquids and solids cannot?

body.back: Gas particles collide with the walls of the container, exerting a force on them.
body.front: Explain how gas pressure is caused.

body.back: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force.
body.front: Explain why gas pressure increases when temperature increases (constant volume).

body.back: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, due to random motion.
body.front: What is diffusion?

body.back: Ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17 vs 36.5), so its particles move faster. Lighter particles diffuse faster.
body.front: Why does ammonia diffuse faster than hydrogen chloride?

o: Particles are close together, irregularly arranged and slide past each other
Particles are far apart, irregularly arranged and move rapidly in all directions
Particles are close together, in a regular arrangement and only vibrate about fixed positions
Particles are far apart, in a regular arrangement and slide past each other
body.q: Which statement correctly describes the arrangement and movement of particles in a liquid?
body.why: In a liquid the particles touch, have no regular pattern and can move past one another, which lets the liquid flow.

o: Sublimation
Condensation
Evaporation
Melting
body.q: What is the name of the change of state when a solid turns directly into a gas?
body.why: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state.

o: It stays constant because the energy supplied is used to overcome forces between particles
It rises more slowly because the particles lose kinetic energy
It stays constant because the particles stop moving
It rises because the particles gain kinetic energy
body.q: A sample of pure water is heated steadily from 80 °C to 120 °C at atmospheric pressure. What happens to the temperature while the water is boiling at 100 °C?
body.why: During a change of state the energy supplied breaks attractions between particles instead of raising their average kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant.

o: Bromine vapour spreads to fill a gas jar of air
A gas can be compressed into a smaller volume
A gas has a lower density than a solid
A gas exerts pressure on a balloon
body.q: Which observation provides evidence that particles in a gas are in constant random motion?
body.why: Diffusion of bromine through air shows that gas particles move randomly and mix without stirring.

o: Closer to the hydrogen chloride end
Closer to the ammonia end
Exactly in the middle of the tube
Evenly along the whole tube
body.q: Ammonia gas (Mr = 17) and hydrogen chloride gas (Mr = 36.5) are released at opposite ends of a long glass tube. A white ring of ammonium chloride forms. Where does the ring form?
body.why: Ammonia particles are lighter and diffuse faster, so they travel further and meet hydrogen chloride nearer the hydrogen chloride end.

o: It increases because the particles move faster and hit the walls more often and with more force
It decreases because the particles move further apart
It stays the same because the number of particles is unchanged
It increases because the particles become larger
body.q: What happens to the pressure of a fixed mass of gas in a sealed container of fixed volume when its temperature is increased?
body.why: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so collisions with the walls are more frequent and more forceful.

o: Condensation
Melting
Boiling
Sublimation of solid to gas
body.q: Which change of state is an exothermic process?
body.why: Condensation releases energy to the surroundings as attractions form between particles, whereas melting, boiling and sublimation absorb energy.

o: Liquid
Solid
Gas
A mixture of solid and gas
body.q: A pure substance melts at 45 °C and boils at 190 °C. What is its physical state at 100 °C?
body.why: 100 °C is above the melting point and below the boiling point, so the substance is a liquid.

o: Its particles have very weak forces between them and move randomly at high speed
Its particles are larger than those in a liquid
Its particles are arranged in a regular pattern
Its particles have stronger forces between them than in a liquid
body.q: Why does a gas, unlike a liquid, fill the whole of its container?
body.why: Negligible attractions and fast random motion let gas particles spread out to occupy all available space.

o: Its particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and can only vibrate
Its particles move freely throughout the solid
Its particles are far apart with weak forces between them
Its particles slide over each other in layers
body.q: Which statement explains why a solid has a fixed shape?
body.why: Strong attractions hold solid particles in fixed positions, so they only vibrate and the solid keeps its shape.
